claims.text: The initial material is a conventional W–Cu composite with discrete tungsten and copper phases and an untreated interface.
A monolayer or few-layer graphene coating can be introduced between the W and Cu phases during fabrication.
The intervention produces a nanoscale graphene interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
Graphene has exceptional thermal conductivity and strong mechanical properties.
A graphene interlayer enhances electron and phonon coupling across the W–Cu interface.
Enhanced electron and phonon coupling lowers W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
Metal–graphene interfaces can strengthen metal composites.
Graphene has robust bonding at the W–Cu boundary.
Graphene resists irradiation-induced damage under fusion-relevant conditions.
The graphene interlayer bridges thermal-expansion differences between tungsten and copper.
The graphene interlayer mitigates irradiation-induced defect formation at the W–Cu boundary.
The graphene-modified W–Cu composite will have higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise identical composite without graphene.
The graphene-modified composite will retain or improve mechanical durability relative to the graphene-free control.
The graphene-modified composite will retain or improve irradiation resistance relative to the graphene-free control.
Temperatures above 1000 °C with neutron or ion irradiation are representative of the proposed fusion-reactor joint conditions.
The benefits depend on adequate adhesion and stability of graphene at the metal interface.
Loss of graphene integrity during thermal cycling or irradiation may eliminate the improvement or degrade performance.
Long-term simultaneous high-temperature and irradiation exposure may cause uncertain graphene performance or interfacial chemical reactions.
A less than 10% conductivity improvement, reduced mechanical durability, or increased irradiation damage relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
